concept.name: SLOs, SLAs & Error Budgets

relationships.description: Connects SLOs, SLAs & Error Budgets to system design hld architectures in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: SLOs set internal reliability targets (e.g., 99.95% availability), SLAs attach legal or financial penalties to external commitments (e.g., 99.9%), and error budgets quantify the exact allowance of bad requests or downtime (1 - SLO) before feature velocity must pause for reliability work.
spark.keyTakeaway: Set your internal SLO tighter than your external SLA so your error budget triggers engineering intervention before customer credits or contract breaches happen.

concept.whyItMatters: Without quantified reliability targets, product teams push risky releases until an outage forces a reactive freeze, or ops teams block all changes in pursuit of an unaffordable 100% uptime. A 99.9% monthly SLO allows 43.8 minutes of downtime (or 100,000 failed requests out of 100M), turning reliability from an emotional argument between Dev and Ops into a shared, measurable budget.
whenToUse: Operating customer-facing APIs, payment gateways, or SaaS platforms where reliability and feature velocity directly compete.
Enforcing automated deployment gates (e.g., Argo Rollouts, Spinnaker) and multi-window burn-rate alerts in Prometheus or OpenTelemetry.
Negotiating realistic tier guarantees with enterprise customers by backing external SLAs with stricter internal SLOs.
whenNotToUse: Early-stage prototypes or pre-product-market-fit MVPs with a handful of test users where instrumentation overhead outweighs signal.
Offline, best-effort batch scripts or internal ad-hoc tooling with no downstream consumers or latency expectations.
Low-traffic endpoints (<10 requests/minute) where a single failed health check or transient blip immediately blows a short-window error budget.
keyPoints: SLI (Service Level Indicator) is the raw ratio: good events divided by valid total events (e.g., HTTP responses with status < 500 and latency < 300ms).
SLO (Service Level Objective) is the target percentage over a rolling or calendar window (e.g., 99.95% over 30 days = 21.9 minutes of allowed downtime).
Error Budget = 100% - SLO; when remaining budget hits zero, feature deploys freeze and engineering shifts to reliability fixes.
SLAs (Service Level Agreements) are external contracts with financial remedies (e.g., 10% service credit below 99.9%) and must always be looser than internal SLOs.
Multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerting (e.g., 14.4x burn over 1h AND 5m) catches fast outages in minutes while ignoring brief, harmless spikes.

examples.title: Checkout API Canary Gating with Error Budgets
examples.scenario: A payments service handles 50M requests/month with a 99.95% availability SLO (25,000 allowed 5xx errors). A buggy release pushes 5xx rate to 1.2% during a 10% canary.
examples.outcome: Prometheus recording rules detect a 24x burn rate within 5 minutes, Argo Rollouts automatically aborts the canary, and 96% of the monthly error budget remains intact.

examples.title: Enterprise SaaS SLA vs. Internal SLO Buffer
examples.scenario: An enterprise analytics vendor signs a 99.9% monthly uptime SLA (43.8 min/month) with 15% fee credits, while operating an internal 99.95% SLO (21.9 min/month).
examples.outcome: When a regional Redis failover consumes 18 minutes of downtime, the team hits 82% of its internal budget and halts schema migrations—avoiding an SLA breach and customer refunds.

tradeOffs.pro: Each additional 'nine' cuts allowed monthly downtime by 10x (from 43.8 min to 4.38 min), satisfying strict enterprise workloads.
tradeOffs.con: Requires multi-region active-active replication, automated failover, and conservative release freezes that can double infrastructure and ops costs.

tradeOffs.pro: A 30-day rolling window smoothly ages out old incidents and keeps teams accountable every day rather than resetting magically on the 1st.
tradeOffs.con: Calendar windows (1st–31st) are harder to game-proof operationally, though they align better with monthly customer billing and SLA credit cycles.

tradeOffs.pro: Request-based SLIs (good requests / total requests) weight peak-hour outages accurately when 10x more users are affected.
tradeOffs.con: Time-based SLIs (good minutes / total minutes) are simpler to compute for low-traffic services where request counts fluctuate wildly.

failureModes.name: Alert Fatigue from Static Thresholds
failureModes.description: Paging on-call whenever 5xx > 0.1% for 5 minutes fires during minor background noise that would take days to exhaust the budget.
failureModes.mitigation: Use Google SRE multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerts (e.g., page only if 1h burn >= 14.4x AND 5m burn >= 14.4x, consuming 2% of the 30-day budget in 1 hour).

failureModes.name: Vanity SLOs (100% or Unmeasured Dependencies)
failureModes.description: Setting a 100% target or measuring only load-balancer 200 OKs while ignoring 12-second p99 timeouts masks real user pain.
failureModes.mitigation: Define composite SLIs combining availability (non-5xx) AND latency (under threshold) measured as close to the client or API gateway as possible.

failureModes.name: Low-Traffic Denominator Distortion
failureModes.description: At 2 requests/minute overnight, 3 failed requests create a 25% error rate for 5 minutes and trigger false-positive error budget pages.
failureModes.mitigation: Add a minimum request volume guard (e.g., `sum(rate(http_requests_total[1h])) > 10`) or pad with synthetic blackbox probes.

failureModes.name: Toothless Error Budget Policy
failureModes.description: Teams track SLO dashboards in Grafana but override deployment freezes every sprint to hit product deadlines.
failureModes.mitigation: Get executive sign-off on a binding error budget policy—automate CI/CD deploy blocks when remaining budget drops below 0% unless an incident-fix flag is set.

commonMistakes: Copying an external SLA (99.9%) directly as the internal SLO with zero safety margin.
Counting client-side 4xx errors (400 Bad Request, 404 Not Found) as server failures in the availability SLI.
Averaging latency across endpoints instead of using histogram percentiles (p95/p99) per critical user journey.
Forgetting that downstream dependencies cap your maximum theoretical SLO (three serial 99.9% services yield at best 99.7%).
Treating error budgets as a target to stay far away from rather than a resource to spend on controlled chaos testing and faster shipping.

sections.content:
## The idea

Every production system faces a permanent tension between **shipping speed** and **stability**. SLIs, SLOs, and Error Budgets replace subjective arguments with a shared mathematical contract:

- **SLI (Service Level Indicator):** A carefully defined quantitative measure of service behavior, almost always expressed as a ratio: `Good Events / Valid Events` (excluding 4xx client errors or health-check noise). Example: proportion of `/v1/orders` HTTP requests returning `< 500` within `250ms`.
- **SLO (Service Level Objective):** The target reliability threshold for an SLI over a measurement window (typically 28 or 30 rolling days). Example: `99.95%` over 30 days.
- **Error Budget:** The inverse of the SLO (`100% - SLO`). For a `99.95%` SLO over 30 days (43,200 minutes), the budget is `0.05%`—exactly **21.6 minutes** of total outage or **50,000 failed requests** per 100M requests.
- **SLA (Service Level Agreement):** A legal contract with customers specifying consequences (service credits, refunds, termination rights) if reliability falls below a looser threshold (e.g., `99.9%`).

Instead of treating every error as a failure, an error budget treats reliability as a **spendable asset**. If the budget is healthy, teams ship fast and run chaos experiments. If the budget is exhausted, non-emergency feature releases pause until reliability work restores margin.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider an **Order Checkout API** serving `2,000 req/s` (~5.184 billion requests per 30-day rolling window) with a **99.95% availability + latency SLO** (`status < 500` and `duration <= 300ms`).

1. **Budget calculation:** `0.05% * 5.184B = 2,592,000` allowed bad requests per 30 days (or `86,400` bad requests/day at steady load).
2. **Burn rate definition:** A burn rate of `1x` consumes 100% of the 30-day budget in exactly 30 days (`0.05%` error rate). A burn rate of `14.4x` (`0.72%` error rate) consumes **2% of the monthly budget in 1 hour** and would exhaust the entire month in 50 hours.
3. **Multi-window alerting (Sloth / Prometheus):** At `14:00 UTC`, a database connection-pool leak pushes the bad-request ratio to `0.9%` (`18x` burn rate).
   - Both the **1-hour window** and **5-minute short window** exceed `14.4x` burn rate by `14:06 UTC`.
   - Alertmanager pages the primary on-call engineer via PagerDuty (`Severity: Page`).
4. **Automated mitigation & budget accounting:** At `14:14 UTC`, the engineer rolls back the bad deployment. Total incident duration is 14 minutes at `18x` burn, consuming `14m * 18 / 43,200m = 0.58%` of the monthly budget.
5. **Reset prevention:** Because the 5-minute window drops back below `14.4x` immediately after rollback, the page auto-resolves without flapping, leaving `99.42%` of the monthly budget intact.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / SLI math and multi-window burn rates
sections.content:
## SLI math and multi-window burn rates

Alerting on raw error percentages fails because a `1%` error rate is catastrophic for a `99.99%` service (`100x` burn) but normal for a `98%` batch API (`0.5x` burn). **Burn rate** normalizes alerts to the SLO:

`Burn Rate = Observed Error Ratio / (1 - SLO)`

Google SRE's standard multi-window pairing prevents both **slow detection** and **slow reset**:

- **Page (2% budget in 1h):** `1h burn >= 14.4x` AND `5m burn >= 14.4x`. Detects a 100% outage in ~2 minutes and resolves within 5 minutes of a fix.
- **Page (5% budget in 6h):** `6h burn >= 6x` AND `30m burn >= 6x`. Catches moderate, sustained degradation (e.g., 0.3% errors on a 99.95% SLO).
- **Ticket (10% budget in 3d):** `3d burn >= 1x` AND `6h burn >= 1x`. Files a Jira/Linear ticket for slow leaks without waking anyone up at 3 AM.

## The 'nines' budget and cost matrix

| SLO Target | Allowed Error Ratio | 30-Day Downtime | 7-Day Downtime | Typical Architecture Required |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **99.0%** | 1.0% | 7h 12m | 1h 40m | Single-region, manual failover, scheduled maintenance windows |
| **99.9%** | 0.1% | 43m 12s | 10m 05s | Multi-AZ active-passive, automated health checks, rolling deploys |
| **99.95%** | 0.05% | 21m 36s | 5m 02s | Multi-AZ active-active, automated canary rollbacks, zero-downtime DB migrations |
| **99.99%** | 0.01% | 4m 19s | 1m 00s | Multi-region failover, strict change freezes, load shedding, chaos testing |
| **99.999%** | 0.001% | 25.9s | 6.0s | Active-active multi-region with automated traffic steering and hardware redundancy |

## Failure modes

- **Dependency Chain Multiplication:** If your API synchronously calls three downstream services each with a `99.9%` SLO, your combined ceiling is `0.999^3 = 99.7%` unless you add fallbacks, caches, or async queues.
- **Reset Lag on Single-Window Alerts:** Alerting on a single 1-hour window keeps firing for up to 55 minutes after an outage is fixed; always pair with a short window (1/12th of the long window).
- **Metric Cardinality Explosion:** Adding `user_id` or `request_id` labels to Prometheus SLI histograms crashes TSDB memory. Restrict SLI labels to `service`, `route`, `method`, and `status_class`.
- **Silent Client-Side Failures:** Measuring SLIs only inside the origin pod misses DNS failures, TLS handshake drops, and CDN/ALB 502s. Measure at the edge or via synthetic probes.

## Error budget policy in practice

An error budget only works when paired with a **pre-agreed escalation policy** signed off by Engineering and Product before an incident occurs:

1. **Budget > 25% remaining:** Normal feature velocity; teams may run controlled fault-injection tests.
2. **Budget 1%–25% remaining:** Require peer review on high-risk config/schema changes; prioritize top reliability debt items in the next sprint.
3. **Budget <= 0% (Exhausted):** Freeze all non-reliability feature deployments; route 100% of engineering capacity to P0/P1 postmortem actions, automated rollbacks, or dependency circuit breakers until the rolling window recovers.
4. **Single-Incident Cap:** If one catastrophic incident consumes >20% of the monthly budget, mandate a blameless postmortem with at least one automated prevention guardrail (e.g., canary check, rate limit) before resuming normal deploys.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Identify 1–3 critical user journeys per service (e.g., login, checkout, search) rather than tracking every internal route.
- [ ] Express every SLI as `good_events / valid_events` excluding `4xx` client errors and health-check noise.
- [ ] Set internal SLOs strictly tighter than external SLAs (e.g., `99.95%` SLO for a `99.9%` SLA).
- [ ] Implement multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerts using Sloth or Pyrra in Prometheus (`1h/5m` at `14.4x`, `6h/30m` at `6x`).
- [ ] Add a minimum traffic threshold on burn-rate alerts so low-volume overnight periods don't trigger false pages.
- [ ] Publish a written Error Budget Policy defining exact deploy-freeze triggers and executive override rules.

nodes.label: Alertmanager / PagerDuty
nodes.role: Pages only on fast multi-window burn

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: SLOs set internal reliability targets (e.g., 99.95% availability), SLAs attach legal or financial penalties to external commitments (e.g., 99.9%), and error budgets quantify the exact allowance of bad requests or downtime (1 - SLO) before feature velocity must pause for reliability work.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Alertmanager / PagerDuty applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Argo Rollouts / CI Gate.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Argo Rollouts / CI Gate experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Use Google SRE multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerts (e.g., page only if 1h burn >= 14.4x AND 5m burn >= 14.4x, consuming 2% of the 30-day budget in 1 hour).

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Set your internal SLO tighter than your external SLA so your error budget triggers engineering intervention before customer credits or contract breaches happen.
Avoid trap: Copying an external SLA (99.9%) directly as the internal SLO with zero safety margin.
Avoid trap: Counting client-side 4xx errors (400 Bad Request, 404 Not Found) as server failures in the availability SLI.
When to reach for it: Operating customer-facing APIs, payment gateways, or SaaS platforms where reliability and feature velocity directly compete.
When to reach for it: Enforcing automated deployment gates (e.g., Argo Rollouts, Spinnaker) and multi-window burn-rate alerts in Prometheus or OpenTelemetry.

putItTogether.title: Putting Slo Sla Error Budgets Together
putItTogether.summary: Set your internal SLO tighter than your external SLA so your error budget triggers engineering intervention before customer credits or contract breaches happen.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Slo Sla Error Budgets before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Prometheus recording rules detect a 24x burn rate within 5 minutes, Argo Rollouts automatically aborts the canary, and 96% of the monthly error budget remains intact.
